prompt: What is the difference between ortho-hydrogen and para-hydrogen?

choices.text: The nuclear spins are parallel in ortho-H2, antiparallel in para-H2
The electron spins are parallel in ortho-H2, antiparallel in para-H2
choices.why: The two forms differ in the spins of the two nuclei, the protons. The names refer to how the nuclear spins line up.

choices.text: Ortho-H2 is vibrating and para-H2 is not
choices.why: Vibration has nothing to do with it. Ortho-H2 has parallel nuclear spins and para-H2 antiparallel ones.

choices.text: Ortho-H2 has a shorter bond than para-H2
choices.why: Both forms have the same bond. They differ only in whether the two nuclear spins are parallel or antiparallel.

explanation: If both nuclear spins are parallel, the molecule is ortho; if they are antiparallel, it is para. The names echo disubstituted benzene, where para means groups at opposite ends.

prompt: H2 has four nuclear spin functions: one singlet and three triplet functions. Which belong to para-hydrogen?

choices.text: The singlet
The three triplet functions
choices.why: The triplet belongs to ortho-H2. Para-H2, with antiparallel nuclear spins, has the single singlet function.

choices.text: Two of the triplet functions
choices.why: The triplet functions all belong to ortho-H2. Para-H2 has only the singlet.

choices.text: All four functions, equally
choices.why: Each function belongs to one form only: the singlet to para-H2 and the three triplet functions to ortho-H2.

explanation: Para-hydrogen has the singlet nuclear spin function, α(1)β(2) − α(2)β(1). The three triplet functions belong to ortho-hydrogen, which is why ortho states carry a weight of 3.

prompt: Which of these nuclear spin functions of H2 is the singlet?

choices.why: With a plus sign the function is unchanged when the nuclei swap, so it is one of the triplet functions. The singlet has a minus sign.
Both spins are α here, so this is a triplet function. The singlet is α(1)β(2) − α(2)β(1).
Both spins are β here, so this is a triplet function. The singlet is α(1)β(2) − α(2)β(1).

explanation: The singlet is the single combination α(1)β(2) − α(2)β(1). The other three, α(1)α(2), α(1)β(2) + α(2)β(1) and β(1)β(2), make up the triplet.

prompt: Why must the total wavefunction of H2 change sign when its two nuclei are exchanged?

choices.text: Its nuclei, protons, are spin-½ fermions
Its two nuclei carry opposite charges
choices.why: Both nuclei are protons with the same charge. The sign change comes from protons being spin-½ fermions.

choices.text: Its two electrons are paired in the bond
choices.why: The rule here is about exchanging the nuclei. Because the protons are spin-½ fermions, the total wavefunction must be antisymmetric.

choices.text: Its nuclei have zero nuclear spin
choices.why: A proton has spin ½. Spin-zero nuclei, such as ^16O, are bosons and need a symmetric total wavefunction instead.

explanation: A proton is a spin-½ nucleus, a fermion, so the total wavefunction must be antisymmetric to exchange of the nuclei: ψ(1,2) = −ψ(2,1).

prompt: Exchanging the two nuclei of H2 must change the sign of the total wavefunction. Which two parts of the wavefunction together decide whether it does?

choices.text: The nuclear spin and rotational parts
The translational and vibrational parts
choices.why: Translation moves the center of mass and vibration depends only on the bond length, so neither changes when the nuclei swap. The nuclear spin and rotational parts decide.

choices.text: The electronic and translational parts
choices.why: The section says neither the electronic motion nor the translation affects the exchange symmetry. The nuclear spin and rotational parts do.

choices.text: The vibrational and nuclear spin parts
choices.why: Vibration depends only on the internuclear distance, which a swap leaves unchanged. The nuclear spin part is paired with the rotational part.

explanation: Translation, vibration and electronic motion have no effect on the exchange symmetry. So the product of the nuclear spin and rotational wavefunctions must be antisymmetric.

prompt: Why does the vibrational motion of H2 have no effect on how its wavefunction behaves when the nuclei are exchanged?

choices.text: It depends only on the internuclear distance
H2 never vibrates at any temperature
choices.why: H2 does vibrate. Its vibration depends only on the distance between the nuclei, and swapping them leaves that distance unchanged.

choices.text: The vibrational wavefunction always changes sign
choices.why: If it did, it would affect the exchange symmetry. It depends only on the bond length, which the swap leaves the same.

choices.text: Vibration only moves the molecule's center of mass
choices.why: Moving the center of mass is translation. Vibration changes the internuclear distance, which a swap leaves the same.

explanation: Vibrational motion depends on the magnitude of the internuclear distance, which is the same after the nuclei are exchanged. So only the nuclear spin and rotational parts matter for the exchange symmetry.

prompt: Exchanging the two nuclei of H2 turns the molecule end over end. According to the section, what happens to its angles θ and φ?

choices.text: θ becomes π − θ and φ becomes φ + π
θ becomes −θ and φ is unchanged
choices.why: The bond direction is reversed, which sends θ to π − θ and also shifts φ by π.

choices.text: θ is unchanged and φ becomes −φ
choices.why: Reversing the bond changes both angles: θ becomes π − θ and φ becomes φ + π.

choices.text: θ becomes θ + π and φ becomes π − φ
choices.why: The two changes are the other way round: θ becomes π − θ and φ becomes φ + π.

explanation: When the nuclei are interchanged, the bond points the opposite way: θ becomes π − θ and φ becomes φ + π. This is what makes the rotational wavefunction symmetric for even J and antisymmetric for odd J.

prompt: How does a rotational wavefunction of H2 with J = 3 behave when the two nuclei are exchanged?

choices.text: It changes sign
It is unchanged
choices.why: That is true for even J. For odd J, such as J = 3, the rotational wavefunction is antisymmetric and changes sign.

choices.text: It becomes zero
choices.why: The wavefunction doesn't vanish. For odd J it simply changes sign.

choices.text: It is multiplied by 2J + 1 = 7
choices.why: 2J + 1 is the number of states in the level, not an exchange factor. For odd J the wavefunction is multiplied by −1.

explanation: The rotational wavefunction is symmetric for even J and antisymmetric for odd J. J = 3 is odd, so exchanging the nuclei changes its sign.

prompt: How do the three triplet nuclear spin functions of H2, such as α(1)α(2), behave when the nuclei are exchanged?

choices.text: All three are unchanged
All three change sign
choices.why: Changing sign is the behavior of the singlet, α(1)β(2) − α(2)β(1). Swapping the labels in α(1)α(2) gives the same function back.

choices.text: Only α(1)α(2) is unchanged; the other two change sign
choices.why: β(1)β(2) and α(1)β(2) + α(2)β(1) also come back unchanged when labels 1 and 2 are swapped. All three triplet functions are symmetric.

choices.text: They turn into the singlet function
choices.why: Exchange doesn't turn one function into another here. Each triplet function comes back unchanged.

explanation: Swapping labels 1 and 2 leaves α(1)α(2), α(1)β(2) + α(2)β(1) and β(1)β(2) unchanged, so the triplet is symmetric. To make the product antisymmetric, the triplet must pair with antisymmetric, odd-J rotational functions.

prompt: Which rotational levels can para-hydrogen occupy?

choices.text: Only even J: 0, 2, 4, …
Only odd J: 1, 3, 5, …
choices.why: Odd J levels belong to ortho-H2. Para-H2's antisymmetric singlet needs symmetric, even-J rotational functions.
The exchange rule allows only half of the levels to each form. Para-H2 takes the even J levels.

choices.text: Only J = 0
choices.why: J = 0 is the lowest para level, but para-H2 can also be in J = 2, 4 and higher even levels.

explanation: The singlet spin function of para-H2 is antisymmetric. Multiplied by a symmetric, even-J rotational function, it gives the required antisymmetric total.

prompt: What is the lowest rotational level that ortho-hydrogen can occupy?

choices.why: J = 0 is even, so it belongs to para-H2. Ortho-H2 is limited to odd J, starting at J = 1.
J = 2 is even, so it belongs to para-H2. The lowest odd level is J = 1.
J = 3 is allowed for ortho-H2, but J = 1 is lower and is also odd.

explanation: Ortho-H2 pairs its symmetric triplet spin functions with antisymmetric, odd-J rotational functions, so its lowest level is J = 1. Even at very low temperature, ortho-H2 still has rotational energy.

prompt: In q_ortho = 3Σ_(J=1,3,5,…)(2J + 1)exp(−J(J + 1)Θ_R/T), what does the factor 3 count?

choices.text: The three triplet nuclear spin states
The three rotational states of the J = 1 level
choices.why: Those are counted by 2J + 1 inside the sum. The 3 outside multiplies every term: it is the three triplet nuclear spin states.

choices.text: The three directions of translation
choices.why: Translation is in a separate factor, q_trans. The 3 in q_ortho is the number of triplet nuclear spin states.

choices.text: The three vibrational modes of H2
choices.why: A diatomic molecule has only one vibrational mode. The 3 counts the triplet nuclear spin states of ortho-H2.

explanation: Every ortho rotational level comes with three nuclear spin states, the triplet, so the whole sum is multiplied by 3. In q_para the factor is 1, for the single singlet state.

prompt: At thermal equilibrium, what happens to the ortho:para ratio N_o/N_p as T → 0?

choices.text: It falls to 0, so the gas becomes all para-H2
It approaches 3
choices.why: 3 is the high-temperature limit. As T → 0, molecules settle into J = 0, which is a para level.

choices.text: It approaches 1
choices.why: There is no reason for equal amounts. At very low temperature only J = 0 is populated, and J = 0 belongs to para-H2.

choices.text: It grows without limit, so the gas becomes all ortho-H2
choices.why: Ortho-H2's lowest level, J = 1, lies above para-H2's J = 0. At equilibrium near 0 K the molecules are in J = 0, which is para.

explanation: At low temperature only the lowest rotational level, J = 0, is populated, and it is a para level. So the equilibrium ratio N_o/N_p goes to 0 as T → 0.

prompt: At high temperature the equilibrium ratio N_o/N_p approaches 3. Where does the 3 come from?

choices.text: The two sums become equal, leaving the triplet's 3
Odd-J levels have three times the energy of even-J levels
choices.why: Energies only enter through the Boltzmann factors, and at high T the odd and even sums become equal. The 3 is the number of triplet spin states.

choices.text: The J = 1 level is three-fold degenerate
choices.why: That 2J + 1 degeneracy is inside the sums, which become equal at high T. The 3 that is left over counts the triplet nuclear spin states.

choices.text: Ortho-H2 molecules rotate three times faster
choices.why: The ratio isn't about rotation speed. At high T the two sums are equal, and the factor 3 from the triplet remains.

explanation: N_o/N_p is 3 × (sum over odd J) divided by (sum over even J). At high temperature the two sums become equal, so the ratio tends to 3, the number of triplet spin states per singlet.

prompt: When the rotational heat capacity of hydrogen was measured at low temperatures, it did not match the equilibrium calculation. Which calculation did it match?

choices.text: A fixed 3:1 mixture of ortho-H2 and para-H2
Pure para-hydrogen
choices.why: Without a catalyst, the cooled gas still holds three ortho-H2 molecules for every para-H2 molecule. The data matched that 3:1 mixture.

choices.text: Pure ortho-hydrogen
choices.why: The gas still contains one para-H2 molecule for every three ortho-H2 molecules. The data matched the fixed 3:1 mixture.

choices.text: A fixed 1:1 mixture of ortho-H2 and para-H2
choices.why: The mixture keeps its high-temperature ratio, 3:1, not 1:1. The data followed (3/4)C_V(ortho) + (1/4)C_V(para).

explanation: The measured heat capacity agreed with (3/4)C_V(ortho) + (1/4)C_V(para). The gas was a frozen high-temperature mixture, three parts ortho-H2 to one part para-H2.

prompt: Hydrogen is cooled from room temperature without a catalyst. Why does it keep an ortho:para ratio of 3:1 instead of reaching the equilibrium ratio?

choices.text: Ortho–para conversion is extremely slow
3:1 is the equilibrium ratio at every temperature
choices.why: The equilibrium ratio falls toward 0 as T drops. The gas keeps 3:1 only because the ortho → para conversion is so slow.

choices.text: Cooling turns para-H2 into ortho-H2 just as fast
choices.why: Equilibrium at low T favors para-H2, not ortho-H2. The ratio stays at 3:1 because conversion in either direction is extremely slow.

choices.text: Ortho-H2 and para-H2 have the same rotational levels
choices.why: They don't: ortho-H2 has odd J and para-H2 even J. The ratio is stuck because the ortho → para conversion rate is very small.

explanation: The ortho → para interconversion rate is very small, so the gas keeps its high-temperature composition, 0.75 ortho-H2 and 0.25 para-H2. It reaches equilibrium only with a catalyst.

prompt: What does adding activated charcoal to cold hydrogen gas do?

choices.text: It catalyzes the ortho–para conversion
It absorbs the ortho-H2 molecules and removes them
choices.why: The section describes charcoal as a catalyst. It speeds up ortho–para conversion so the gas reaches its equilibrium composition.

choices.text: It locks the ortho:para ratio at 3:1
choices.why: Without a catalyst the ratio stays at 3:1. Charcoal does the opposite: it lets the gas reach the equilibrium ratio.

choices.text: It warms the gas back up to room temperature
choices.why: The charcoal doesn't heat the gas. It catalyzes ortho–para conversion, and the measured heat capacity then follows the equilibrium curve.

explanation: A catalyst such as activated charcoal speeds up the ortho–para conversion. With it, the gas reaches the equilibrium composition, and measurements follow the curve labeled eq.

prompt: The section calls the heat capacity of hydrogen a very nice case where experiment supports the methods of statistical thermodynamics. What else does it support?

choices.text: The antisymmetry principle for bosons and fermions
The equipartition principle at all temperatures
choices.why: Equipartition fails at low temperature. The hydrogen data support the antisymmetry principle for bosons and fermions.

choices.text: The ideal gas law at low temperature
choices.why: The case isn't about pressure and volume. It shows that the rules for exchanging identical nuclei, the antisymmetry principle, are right.

choices.text: The rule that nuclear spins never affect chemistry
choices.why: The case shows the opposite: nuclear spins change the rotational populations and the heat capacity. It supports the antisymmetry principle.

explanation: The ortho and para heat capacities follow from the requirement that the total wavefunction be antisymmetric to exchange of the protons. Their agreement with experiment supports both statistical thermodynamics and the antisymmetry principle.

prompt: On a macroscopic scale, which measured properties of hydrogen are affected by its nuclear spins?

choices.text: Its entropy and heat capacity
Its molar mass and density
choices.why: Ortho-H2 and para-H2 have the same mass. The nuclear spins change the rotational populations, which shows up in the entropy and heat capacity.

choices.text: Its bond length and bond energy
choices.why: The nuclear spins don't change the electronic or vibrational motion. They change which rotational levels are used, affecting entropy and heat capacity.

choices.text: Its color and electrical conductivity
choices.why: Hydrogen's nuclear spins don't change these. They affect the rotational populations, and so the measured entropy and heat capacity.

explanation: Nuclear spins decide which rotational levels each form can occupy. On a macroscopic scale this shows up in measured entropies and heat capacities.

prompt: The section writes the total partition function of H2 as a product of factors. Besides q_elec, q_vib, q_rot and q_trans, which factor does it include?

choices.text: q_nuc, for the nuclear spins
q_inter, for forces between molecules
choices.why: The molecules are treated as independent, so there is no such factor. The extra factor is q_nuc, for the nuclear spins.

choices.text: q_ion, for ionized molecules
choices.why: Ionization isn't part of this partition function. The extra factor is q_nuc, for the two nuclear spins.

choices.text: A second q_rot, for each nucleus
choices.why: Rotation of the molecule is counted once in q_rot. The extra factor is q_nuc, for the nuclear spins.

explanation: The section writes q_tot = q_elec q_vib q_rot q_trans q_nuc. For H2, the nuclear spin factor can't be treated separately from q_rot, because the spin state decides which J levels are allowed.

prompt: A ^16O nucleus has zero nuclear spin. How must the total wavefunction of ^16O2 behave when its two nuclei are exchanged?

choices.text: It must stay the same
It must change sign
choices.why: That is the rule for spin-½ nuclei, such as the protons in H2. A spin-zero nucleus is a boson, which needs a symmetric wavefunction.

choices.text: It may either stay the same or change sign
choices.why: Identical nuclei don't get a choice. Spin-zero nuclei are bosons, and only symmetric wavefunctions are permitted for bosons.

choices.text: It must become zero
choices.why: The wavefunction doesn't vanish. For bosons, such as spin-zero ^16O nuclei, it must stay the same.

explanation: A ^16O nucleus has zero spin, so it is a boson. Only symmetric wavefunctions are permitted for bosons, so the total wavefunction must be unchanged by the exchange.

prompt: Which rotational levels of ^16O2 contribute to its rotational partition function?

choices.text: Only odd J: 1, 3, 5, …
Only even J: 0, 2, 4, …
choices.why: That would be right if the rest of the molecule's wavefunction were symmetric. O2's ground electronic state is antisymmetric to exchange of the nuclei, so only odd J occur.

choices.text: Every J, each with a weight of 3
choices.why: ^16O nuclei have zero spin, so there are no nuclear spin states to give a weight of 3. Only the odd J levels contribute.

choices.text: Every J, as for a heteronuclear molecule
choices.why: The two ^16O nuclei are identical, so exchange symmetry removes half of the levels. Only odd J occur.

explanation: The spin-zero ^16O nuclei are bosons, so the total wavefunction must be symmetric. O2's ground electronic state is antisymmetric to the exchange, so the rotational part must be antisymmetric too, which allows only odd J.

prompt: The rotational energy of H2 in level J is E_J = J(J + 1)k_B Θ_R, with Θ_R = 87.6 K. The lowest ortho level is J = 1 and the lowest para level is J = 0. How far apart are they, expressed as a temperature, E/k_B, in K? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: E/k_B = J(J + 1)Θ_R = 1 × 2 × 87.6 K = 175.2 K above J = 0. Ortho-H2 can never drop below this level, which is why equilibrium hydrogen turns into para-H2 at low temperature.

prompt: At low temperature, keeping only the J = 1 and J = 0 terms, the equilibrium ratio of hydrogen is N_o/N_p ≈ 9 exp(−2Θ_R/T). With Θ_R = 87.6 K, what is N_o/N_p at 43.8 K? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: 2Θ_R/T = 2 × 87.6/43.8 = 4, so N_o/N_p ≈ 9 exp(−4) = 9 × 0.0183 = 0.165. The 9 is 3 nuclear spin states times 3 rotational states of J = 1; at equilibrium only about 14% of the molecules are ortho-H2 at this temperature.

prompt: H2's combined rotational and nuclear spin partition function is q = S_even + 3S_odd, where S_even and S_odd are the sums of (2J + 1)exp(−J(J + 1)Θ_R/T) over even J and over odd J. At a certain temperature, S_even = 1.01 and S_odd = 0.41. What is q? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: q = 1.01 + 3 × 0.41 = 1.01 + 1.23 = 2.24. The odd-J sum is weighted by 3 for the triplet nuclear spin states, the even-J sum by 1 for the singlet.

prompt: Hydrogen cooled without a catalyst has the rotational heat capacity C_V = (3/4)C_V(ortho) + (1/4)C_V(para). At 150 K the calculated values are C_V(ortho) = 1.9 J/(mol·K) and C_V(para) = 11.7 J/(mol·K). What is C_V of this mixture, in J/(mol·K)? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: C_V = (3/4)(1.9) + (1/4)(11.7) = 1.425 + 2.925 = 4.35 J/(mol·K). The weights are the high-temperature fractions, 0.75 ortho-H2 and 0.25 para-H2, which stay frozen on cooling.

prompt: A 2.00 mol sample of hydrogen is at equilibrium at room temperature, where N_o/N_p has reached its high-temperature value of 3. How many moles of para-H2 does it contain? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: With three ortho-H2 molecules for every para-H2 molecule, para-H2 is 1/4 of the total. 2.00 mol × 1/4 = 0.500 mol of para-H2, and 1.50 mol is ortho-H2.

prompt: In q_ortho, each odd-J level carries the weight 3(2J + 1): 3 nuclear spin states times 2J + 1 rotational states. How many states in total belong to the J = 3 level of ortho-H2?
explanation: 3 × (2 × 3 + 1) = 3 × 7 = 21 states. A para level has only the 2J + 1 rotational states, since the singlet has just one nuclear spin state.
